summary: Provides extensions to the PCE Communication Protocol to support the GMPLS control plane, addressing requirements identified in RFC 7025. This lets path computation work for Generalized MPLS networks, not only MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: PCEP is the protocol a router uses to ask a path computation element for a route. This RFC teaches PCEP about GMPLS networks, where the traffic is light, the bandwidth is measured in wavelengths or time slots, and the labels are technology specific.

what is a generalized endpoint in pcep
subtitle: Adds GMPLS path computation to PCEP, with generalized bandwidth, endpoints, labels and protection attributes.

tldr.problem: The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) can ask a Path Computation Element for a path, but its existing objects describe MPLS networks and cannot express the bandwidth, labels, endpoints and protection that GMPLS networks need.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a capability TLV, three new object types, a routing granularity flag, label subobjects for the include and exclude route objects, a protection attribute TLV, extra error codes and new NO-PATH reasons, all reachable only after both peers advertise GMPLS support.
tldr.outcome: A PCE can now compute paths over optical and other GMPLS networks, with the bandwidth and label detail those networks require. The RFC is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8779 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2020. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9756. It addresses the GMPLS requirements listed in RFC 7025.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs GMPLS Extensions
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths on behalf of other routers, and PCEP is the protocol a Path Computation Client (PCC) uses to talk to it. The architecture for both MPLS and GMPLS networks is defined in RFC 4655, but most of the existing PCEP RFCs, including RFC 5440, RFC 5521, RFC 5541 and RFC 5520, were written for MPLS networks. They do not cover the range of GMPLS networks, such as Optical Transport Networks and Wavelength Switched Optical Networks.

This RFC supplies the missing extensions. The functional requirements it addresses are listed in RFC 7025 and RFC 7449. It adds new object types, TLVs, encodings, error codes and procedures, and it does not change the existing PCEP grammar: the PCReq and PCRep messages stay as they are.

The extensions cover several gaps. Two new object types are added to the BANDWIDTH object, one to the LOAD-BALANCING object and one to the END-POINTS object. A new TLV is added to the Open message for capability negotiation, and another to the LSPA object. The Label subobject is now allowed in the IRO and XRO objects, and a new flag in the RP object records the routing granularity used in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP was built for IP networks. This RFC adds the objects and fields needed to compute paths over optical and other GMPLS networks.

sections.title: What GMPLS Path Computation Needs
sections.content:
The requirements come from RFC 7025 and fall into a few groups. First, the network has to know what is being switched: a switching type such as Layer 2 Switch Capable or Time-Division Multiplex Capable, an encoding type such as Ethernet or SONET/SDH, and sometimes a signal type. Second, some switching technologies need traffic parameters of their own. In SDH/SONET and OTN networks the concatenation type and the concatenation number change both the data that is switched and the link that can carry it, and they are described together.

Third, a request may ask for more bandwidth in one direction than the other. Fourth, a GMPLS network has interfaces without addresses, so unnumbered interface identifiers have to be supported. Fifth, labels are technology specific: a wavelength label in a WSON network, or the label restriction that RSVP-TE allows. Finally, a client has to be able to say how much detail it wants back in the path, at the level of a node, a link or a label, which is what RSVP-TE calls explicit label control.

The RFC maps each requirement to the PCEP object that carries it, so a reader can see which object answers which requirement: switching, encoding and signal types go with the TE-LSP and its endpoints, concatenation goes with the BANDWIDTH object, protection types with the LSPA object, and labels with the END-POINTS, IRO, XRO and RRO objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical networks need more than an IP network does: they switch different kinds of signal, measure bandwidth in wavelengths or time slots, and use labels that depend on the technology. This section lists what a request has to be able to say.

sections.title: Announcing GMPLS Capability
sections.content:
GMPLS support has to be discovered before it is used. The IGP-based PCE Discovery protocol of RFC 5088 and RFC 5089 already has a bit in the PCE-CAP-FLAGS Sub-TLV for path computation with GMPLS link constraints, and a PCE that sets it must then qualify the level of support during the PCEP session.

That is what the new GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV, type 45, does. A speaker that supports these extensions must include the TLV in the Open message. If one of the peers leaves the TLV out, the peers must not use any of the objects and TLVs defined in this RFC. A speaker that supports the extensions but did not advertise the capability, and then receives a message using them, must generate a PCEP error with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 31, and should terminate the session.

The TLV carries a Flags field, and this document defines no flags in it. Unassigned flags must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends of a PCEP session have to say that they handle GMPLS before they use the new fields. If one end does not, the session must not use them at all.

sections.title: Generalized Bandwidth and Load Balancing
sections.content:
The BANDWIDTH object carries the size of the traffic-engineered LSP, and the two object types defined in RFC 5440 do not describe GMPLS bandwidth well enough. The RFC therefore adds object type 3, Generalized bandwidth, and object type 4, Generalized bandwidth of an existing TE-LSP for which a reoptimization is requested. Both reuse the RSVP-TE traffic specification encoding, so they can express asymmetric bandwidth and the GMPLS parameters of SDH/SONET, G.709, ATM and MEF networks.

Each object has a Bw Spec Type field, which corresponds to the C-Type values of the RSVP-TE SENDER_TSPEC object: 2 for Intserv, 4 for SONET/SDH, 5 for G.709, 6 for Ethernet, 7 for OTN-TDM and 8 for SSON. A 16-bit Bandwidth Spec Length gives the length of the generalized bandwidth and must be greater than zero; the 16-bit Reverse Bandwidth Spec Length gives the length of the reverse direction and may be zero. A client asking for symmetric bandwidth should leave the reverse length at zero, and a client asking for asymmetric bandwidth should fill in both directions.

The LOAD-BALANCING object asks for a set of at most a given number of TE-LSPs that together carry a given bandwidth. Its new object type 2, Generalized Load Balancing, follows the same encoding, with a Max-LSP field for the number of paths and a minimum bandwidth spec for each of them. The meaning does not change: if the total bandwidth and the minimum bandwidth can be reduced to scalars, the sum over the set of TE-LSPs is greater than the requested bandwidth. The mapping of a bandwidth onto a number of paths is left to each transport technology. When the PCE cannot handle the two bandwidth types at once, it must return NO-PATH with the flag that load balancing could not be performed with the bandwidth constraints set.
sections.plainLanguage: The old bandwidth object only counts bits per second. The new one reuses the way RSVP-TE writes traffic specifications, so a request can say how much bandwidth is needed in each direction and in the units of the transport technology.

sections.title: Generalized Endpoints
sections.content:
The END-POINTS object says where a path should start and end. Its new object type 5, Generalized Endpoint, covers three things the old type could not: a source and a destination of different endpoint types, label restrictions on the endpoint, and unnumbered endpoints as seen in GMPLS networks.

The body holds a list of TLVs: IPV4-ADDRESS (39), IPV6-ADDRESS (40), UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT (41), LABEL-REQUEST (42) and LABEL-SET (43). The UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT TLV carries the router ID of the LSR and a 32-bit interface ID. The LABEL-REQUEST TLV says how to read the labels that follow, with a switching type, an encoding type and a Generalized Protocol Identifier that names the payload. The LABEL-SET TLV carries the label values or ranges that are allowed, with three new bits: U for the upstream direction of a bidirectional LSP, O for an old label left over from a reoptimization, and L for a loose, that is preferred but not mandatory, set of labels.

An Endpoint Type field says what shape the request has. Value 0 is point-to-point, and values 1 to 4 are point-to-multipoint with the corresponding leaf type. Values 245 to 255 are for experimental use. A PCE that does not support a given endpoint type should answer with Error-Type 4 and Error-value 7.
sections.plainLanguage: The new endpoint object can name an unnumbered interface, put limits on which labels may be used at the ends of the path, and describe a tree rather than a single path.

sections.title: Labels, Exclusions and Protection in the Path
sections.content:
RSVP-TE can carry a label definition inside the path, and the IRO object, which lists things the path must include, now accepts a Label subobject of type 10. The subobject must follow a subobject that identifies a link, either an IP address subobject or an interface ID subobject, and more than one Label subobject may follow each link. If the PCE can allocate labels, for example through explicit label control, it must pick one label from the set of values for that link. If it cannot, it answers with NO-PATH and the bit that no label resource is in range.

The XRO object, which lists things the path must avoid, gains a matching Label subobject of type 10, so a client can exclude specific labels. Its X bit says whether the exclusion is mandatory or merely desired.

The LSPA object, which carries LSP attributes, may carry a new PROTECTION-ATTRIBUTE TLV of type 44. It holds the information of the PROTECTION object of RFC 4872, including the LSP protection flags and the link flags, and a PCE may use those flags as routing policy input. The TLV is optional and a PCE that ignores it must not include it in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: A request can now pin down the label on each link, rule labels out, and tell the PCE what kind of protection the path must have.

sections.title: Reporting Why There Is No Path
sections.content:
When the PCE cannot find a path, it answers with a NO-PATH object, which may carry a NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV that gives the reason. Seven new flags describe GMPLS-specific reasons: protection mismatch, no resource, granularity not supported, no endpoint label resource, no endpoint label resource in range, no label resource in range, and that load balancing could not be performed with the bandwidth constraints.

The RFC also adds error codes. Error-Type 4 (Not supported object) gains values 6, 7, 8 and 9, for an unsupported BANDWIDTH object type, an unsupported endpoint type, an unsupported TLV in the Generalized Endpoint object, and an unsupported granularity in the RP object flags. Error-Type 10 (Reception of an invalid object) gains values 24 to 31, covering a bad bandwidth object, unsupported protection flags, and several LABEL-SET problems. A new Error-Type 29, Path computation failure, reports a constraint the PCE did not understand, for instance a generalized bandwidth value it cannot interpret; if the constraint was understood but no path exists, the PCE uses NO-PATH instead.
sections.plainLanguage: When no path can be found, the answer says why: no resources, a label outside the allowed range, a protection type that does not match, or a constraint the element cannot even read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GMPLS networks carry a high volume of traffic and can be a critical part of a network, so the identity of the PCE and the PCC and the channel between them matter. The RFC lists three attack situations. In PCE identity theft, a client asks a malicious PCE that poses as a real one, and the path it returns may pass through a place the attacker controls, where the traffic can be sniffed, changed or dropped, and may quietly ignore the constraints in the request. In PCC identity theft, a malicious client asks a real PCE for paths and learns enough about the physical topology to plan a later attack. In message inspection, sniffing the PCEP messages gives the same knowledge.

The protections come from the usual mechanisms. RFC 8253 provides origin verification, message integrity and replay protection, and PCEs and PCCs should use it. Against a malicious PCE, the client should hold policies that check the returned path against the constraints it asked for, and a data-plane mechanism can verify the connectivity afterwards.
sections.plainLanguage: A path element that is hijacked can send traffic through a place the attacker controls or ignore the constraints it was given. The protections are the usual ones: secure the channel, and check the path that comes back.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: No flags are defined; unassigned flags are set to zero and ignored on receipt.

viz.caption: The new PCEP TLV types this RFC registers

items.label: IPV4-ADDRESS
items.desc: A numbered endpoint with an IPv4 address.

items.label: IPV6-ADDRESS
items.desc: A numbered endpoint with an IPv6 address.

items.label: UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT
items.desc: An unnumbered interface: router ID plus a 32-bit interface ID.

items.label: LABEL-REQUEST
items.desc: Switching and encoding type that says how to read the labels that follow.

items.label: LABEL-SET
items.desc: The label values or ranges allowed at the endpoint.

items.label: PROTECTION-ATTRIBUTE
items.desc: Protection information carried in the LSPA object.

items.label: GMPLS-CAPABILITY
items.desc: Announces GMPLS support in the Open message.

viz.caption: Bandwidth specification types, taken from the RSVP-TE traffic specification
What the GMPLS extensions add to PCEP

items.title: Generalized bandwidth
items.text: Bandwidth in the units of the transport technology, and different in each direction.

items.title: Generalized load balancing
items.text: A set of paths, with a minimum bandwidth per path, in the same units.

items.title: Generalized endpoint
items.text: Unnumbered interfaces, label limits, and point-to-multipoint trees.

items.title: Routing granularity
items.text: Ask for the path at node, link or label detail.

items.title: Labels in the path
items.text: Include or exclude specific labels on each link.

items.title: Protection attributes
items.text: Tell the PCE what protection the path needs.
